I had just emerged from a cinema in downtown Prague, where I had sat through this film—not because the poster attracted me, with its Hollywood-style heroics that seemed old-fashioned and overwrought, nor because of the celebrated cast, which made me wary, knowing how those highly-starred French productions so often prove pathetic. I went simply because in a city like Prague, films in my mother tongue of French are rare treasures, and because I cherish Adjani, Depardieu, and Rappeneau's magnificent Cyrano. Having seen it, I feel compelled to write this brief commentary, for I find myself disagreeing profoundly with the prevailing opinions on this database.

I was not disappointed, though perhaps not in the way one hopes. The film resembles its poster exactly: the characters prove as stupid as they appear. For a while I imagined that Adjani might be playing caricature, offering us a comic figure at whom we could laugh with knowing pleasure. She is not. Consider the moment when she confesses to Depardieu that she murdered the corpulent man we saw her kill in the opening sequence—suddenly the violins swell in big, fat, pathetic music meant to make us weep and recognize that Adjani's character possesses hidden depths. Perhaps this was humor operating at some tenth level of irony, but I confess my sense of humor fails to reach such heights. If I want amusing French cinema about the Second World War, I watch La Grande Vadrouille again, which is definitively more entertaining.

I have also read here that Lemoine delivers a great performance. I must say I have never witnessed such wretched acting, though admittedly I have never seen an Ed Wood film. Nevertheless, the film is handsomely shot, with many expensive, well-composed scenes—the Panthéon in morning light as the German army enters Paris, the refugees settling on a bridge in Bordeaux. Rappeneau, I believe, is a capable filmmaker who requires a strong script. It was easy with Cyrano, where he didn't have to write the dialogue himself.

I give it one out of ten.

For two decades this programme has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, the violent, the sexually incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious—a parade of degeneracy presented as ordinary existence. Eager to demonstrate to their middle-class peers how intimately familiar they have become with the authentic "working-class," these writers dream up the lumpen rabble that constitutes the citizenry of Eastenders, that fictional square mile of unrelenting misery. This exercise exerts a toxic effect on certain minds less well equipped than others to distinguish fiction from reality, and thus we discover members of the actual population assuming the attitudes, the vocal inflections, the very demeanour of the inhabitants of Walford. Thus it came to pass that Eastenders does indeed mirror life; but only after life itself had been hoodwinked into mirroring Eastenders—a perfect inversion of art and existence. Other soaps have since followed in this programme's footsteps, filled to their stinking gunwhales with ugly, potato-faced, shaven-headed, pot-bellied characters who scowl at one another whilst issuing threats constantly. This remains the proletariat as perceived by writers who produce such trash. These same writers grow rich on the proceeds of their output and proceed to enjoy the finer things of life in their rarified enclaves, while the burgeoning population of new, television-induced drones marches inexorably toward cultural bankruptcy. And there you have the new priests and their creatures.

The common assumption that companies trading over-the-counter lack legitimacy could scarcely be further from the truth. Many enterprises appear on the OTC markets precisely because they have yet to satisfy the stringent requirements imposed by the NASDAQ or the New York Stock Exchange—those bastions of American capital that admit only the most established firms to their trading floors. Consider the NASDAQ, which maintains three distinct sets of listing criteria: a company must satisfy at least one of these three standards while simultaneously meeting the fundamental rules applicable to all prospective entrants.

Yet one should not imagine that the OTC markets operate without regulation, for such a notion would be equally mistaken. While these exchanges impose no minimum thresholds for revenue, profitability, or assets, they nonetheless require audited financial statements alongside continuous filing and reporting to both the Securities and Exchange Commission and the National Association of Securities Dealers. Furthermore, the OTC comprises several distinct tiers—the OTCQX, the OTCQB, and the OTC Pink among them—each governed by its own particular set of standards. Those seeking detailed information about OTC listing requirements might consult the educational resources at otcmarkets.com.

A company choosing to trade over-the-counter undertakes a serious commitment to public status, one requiring substantial financial investment. Presently, the fees associated with securing an OTC listing range from thirty thousand to one hundred fifty thousand dollars, varying according to the firm selected and the scope of services included in their offering. Few would characterize such sums—thirty thousand dollars at minimum—as anything less than a substantial financial commitment.

When I examined the requirements for listing on the Toronto Stock Exchange, the process appeared considerably more streamlined than those governing major American markets, consisting principally of an application, submission of corporate records, and finally a determination rendered by a TSX committee. Additional particulars regarding the Toronto exchange may be found through TMX Group's official resources.

The OTC markets have acquired their tarnished reputation largely through the activities of those "Get Rich on Penny Stocks" enterprises that aggressively promote shares in obscure companies, inducing vast numbers of investors to purchase securities without conducting proper due diligence or examining the company's prospectus. When these speculators inevitably sustain significant losses on poorly-informed investment decisions, they reflexively blame their misfortune on the company's OTC status rather than acknowledging their own investigative failures.

Whether one ultimately chooses to participate in OTC markets, the decision should never rest upon the number of exchanges listing a particular security. Rather, sound investment judgment must derive from thorough, independent research into the company itself—its fundamentals, its management, its prospects. The venue of exchange matters far less than the substance of what is being exchanged.

Consider the proposition that students should be permitted to bring cellular devices to school and use them during lunch periods and unstructured intervals, provided they power them down during instructional hours. The first argument supporting this policy centers on conflict reduction: when adolescents occupy themselves with their phones during midday breaks, their attention diverts from interpersonal tensions that might otherwise escalate into confrontations. Absorbed in their glowing screens, students become less inclined toward the quarrels and social dramas that burden not only themselves but also their teachers, who must mediate these disputes.

The second consideration involves attendance. A significant portion of chronic absenteeism stems from students' reluctance to face confiscation of their devices. Many adolescents, knowing that school regulations will separate them from their phones—perhaps for the third violation, triggering parental notification—simply choose not to attend. They fear the conversation awaiting them at home, the revelation that they were messaging during algebra rather than attending to quadratic equations, the punishment of losing phone privileges until their grade point averages climb back toward acceptability.

This matter deserves serious administrative reflection. Imagine a scenario in which students enjoy phone access during designated free periods: teachers would no longer spend their own precious lunch intervals breaking up altercations in the cafeteria. Instead, they could experience genuine respite from the emotional turbulence that characterizes middle school hallways. Grant students their devices during non-academic time, and both staff and student body might finally breathe easier, stepping back from the theatrical conflicts that define daily life in these buildings.

The article "Driverless Cars Are Coming" examines both the drawbacks and the advantages of autonomous vehicles, a technological advance that captivates the imagination even as it raises unsettling questions about safety and human responsibility. While driverless cars certainly possess an undeniable appeal, one must pause to consider whether they represent genuine progress or merely convenient distraction from fundamental concerns.

Among the most troubling risks stands the possibility of mechanical failure—a malfunction that could send an unwitting passenger careening into collision, helpless before the very technology meant to protect them. The human factor, too, presents complications: when the vehicle assumes control, when the driver becomes mere passenger, drowsiness becomes not merely possible but probable, the rhythmic hum of highway travel lulling consciousness into dangerous repose. Yet the article's section "Driving Or Assisting?" proposes an intriguing countermeasure: entertainment systems and heads-up displays that engage attention during automated driving, features that would shut down instantly when human intervention becomes necessary, summoning the driver back to alertness and command.

The benefits, admittedly, carry considerable weight. Consider the harried professional, late for morning obligations, who might finally consume breakfast during the commute, or attend to grooming rituals abandoned in the rushed moments between shower and departure. Consider, too, the business call that cannot wait, the conversation that current law renders dangerous or illegal without Bluetooth technology—autonomous driving would transform such necessities from hazardous distractions into routine matters conducted safely while in motion.

Yet darker possibilities emerge when convenience breeds irresponsibility. One envisions the weekend reveler who, emboldened by automation, drinks to excess, trusting the vehicle to deliver them home safely—only to face catastrophic malfunction, collision, and the harsh judgment of law enforcement. In such scenarios, legal liability would fall squarely upon the intoxicated passenger, whatever the technological failure, and consequences would follow with swift certainty. These, then, constitute the essential tensions surrounding driverless vehicles: promise shadowed by peril, liberation shadowed by new forms of accountability.

Ben Kingsley inhabits Frank, a hit man in the employ of Russian mobsters who operate from their unlikely stronghold in Buffalo. He is also, crucially and catastrophically, an alcoholic whose dependence has begun to corrode his professional competence. When he succumbs to sleep in his vehicle during what should have been a straightforward assassination, his uncle—who happens also to be his mob superior—dispatches him westward to San Francisco. There Frank must attend Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and secure employment as an assistant in a mortuary. If this arrangement strikes you as utterly devoid of internal logic, rest assured you have not misunderstood. The narrative trajectory that follows manages simultaneously to improve and to deteriorate, though deterioration comes first and with considerable force.

Frank transforms himself, inexplicably and overnight, into a mortician of genuine skill despite possessing no training whatsoever in the funerary arts. Yet his interactions with the bereaved families, with his colleagues at the funeral home, and with fellow sufferers at AA prove unexpectedly compelling. The viewer finds himself hoping for this damaged man's redemption, observing the small, authentic changes taking root in his existence. Luke Wilson appears as Frank's AA sponsor, a casting choice that promises much yet delivers disappointingly little—the character announces his homosexuality, then allows this detail to evaporate into irrelevance, serving no narrative purpose.

The film plummets into true absurdity with the arrival of Tea Leoni's character. She exists in a register of complete unreality, and her romantic entanglement with Frank collapses under the weight of their utter lack of chemistry, two actors occupying the same frame without ever truly meeting. From her entrance onward, Frank himself becomes a less coherent presence, his characterization lurching from one arbitrary choice to another without pattern or psychological consistency. The comedy remains muted throughout, yielding only occasional laughter—a particular disappointment given the cast's established comedic credentials.

Further problems accumulate relentlessly. Kingsley's accent wanders without compass or conviction among Italian, Russian, and Hispanic inflections. Frank confesses his profession as a hired killer to numerous individuals, including an entire AA assembly, yet no one registers alarm or considers involving authorities. The final act resorts to the most exhausted conventions: Leoni's insufferable character pursues Frank through an airport terminal just as he prepares to board his Buffalo-bound flight.

Despite a promising premise and an intriguing opening half-hour, the film collapses into comprehensive disaster, ultimately dissolving into incoherence. Frank commemorates one year of sobriety in the film's closing moments. I anticipate celebrating many years of having erased "You Kill Me" from memory. My assessment: D.

"What do you think I should wear tomorrow?"

"What do you think of this outfit?"

"Would this necklace look good with these shoes?"

Questions such as these echo through countless conversations each day, and perhaps you yourself have posed them more often than you care to admit. The prevailing wisdom holds that multiple opinions invariably prove superior to one, a conviction so widespread that studies reveal more than half of all Americans seek a second opinion before committing to a decision. Consider, for instance, the familiar scenario: you find yourself in a boutique, contemplating an expensive pair of shoes, and you turn to your companion for guidance. Should they demur, you promptly solicit another perspective. According to recent research conducted at Harvard University, this pattern of consultation constitutes not aberrant behavior but rather common practice. Fashion transforms with relentless speed—whether through fast fashion's disposable aesthetics or streetwear's rebellious codes—and people perpetually seek external validation because they experience it as a psychological necessity.

Picture yourself standing before a mirror, trying on an oversized t-shirt that strains conventional notions of proportion and appeal. You might find it attractive; perhaps your friend concurs with enthusiasm. But should you present this garment to your father for his assessment, the response would almost certainly differ. Fathers, as a demographic, harbor profound antipathy toward oversized, ungainly t-shirts. Seeking that second opinion remains advisable regardless, for whether the feedback arrives positive or negative in character, it shapes and refines your capacity to make sound judgments. Yet this principle does not hold universally. Some individuals steadfastly refuse to listen, even when presented with constructive criticism. Research from George Mason University documents a curious paradox: after requesting a second opinion and receiving negative feedback, certain people nevertheless persist in choosing precisely what that feedback warned against. What accounts for this peculiar mentality?

Human beings have evolved across millennia to become the planet's dominant species, and our cognitive architecture reflects this ascendancy. Our minds harbor an inherent conviction of their own correctness, an assumption that others labor under misapprehension. This cognitive bias explains why respecting opposing viewpoints proves so difficult for many; they cannot accept the possibility of their own error. The Federal Bureau of Investigation has reported that even serial killers sought multiple opinions before committing their first murders—though everyone counseled against violence, the killers proceeded regardless, demonstrating how catastrophically judgment can fail despite consultation.

But what of those who never ask for additional perspectives at all? Research conducted by the Virginia Department of Health reveals that individuals suffering from depression, anxiety, and insomnia prove ten times less likely to seek multiple opinions or request advice. Overthinking, shyness, and embarrassment conspire to convince them that only negative feedback awaits, which in turn prevents them from asking altogether. This dynamic contributes significantly to depression's troubling ascendance in contemporary society. People feel imprisoned, abandoned, convinced that not even their closest friends can offer assistance. They fear judgment and humiliation, terrified of appearing wrong or foolish, and this fear paralyzes them. The problem continues to metastasize.

Additional research from Virginia Tech discovered that people who regularly seek advice—those who make consultation a daily practice—overwhelmingly turn to older individuals, drawn by the promise of wisdom and accumulated life experience. Seeking feedback and soliciting multiple opinions remains invaluable whenever you pursue sound guidance or wish to effect improvements in any dimension of your existence. Whether confronting a school assignment, navigating important professional responsibilities, or simply selecting appropriate clothing, room for improvement always exists. Therefore, resist the temptation to avoid consultation; ask multiple people for their perspectives and embrace their feedback with openness and courage.

The long stretch of summer has always belonged to students as a season of release—those sun-drenched months when the weight of examinations and deadlines lifts, when friendships deepen over lazy afternoons and small adventures multiply like fireflies at dusk. Yet certain schools have begun to question whether this interlude should remain entirely free from academic obligation, proposing instead that students undertake projects throughout the vacation to sustain the momentum of learning. The question then becomes one of design: should teachers craft these summer assignments, or should students themselves determine their shape and substance? The superior approach, I would argue, lies in teacher-designed projects—for such assignments prepare students for the curriculum ahead, provide an initial grade upon which to build, and remain mercifully brief in their demands.

Consider first that teachers, intimately familiar with the territory they will traverse in the coming year, can construct projects that introduce specific units with precision and care. This preview of subject matter serves a dual purpose: it kindles early interest in topics not yet formally encountered, and it establishes foundational knowledge before the first bell rings. When September arrives and instruction begins in earnest, students who have completed such preparatory work possess an advantage, however modest—a foothold in unfamiliar terrain. That initial familiarity, even slight, can determine whether a student merely survives a challenging course or genuinely flourishes within it.

Furthermore, when teachers design summer projects, they retain the authority to transform these assignments into actual grades, allowing students to commence the academic year with achievement already recorded in the gradebook. This prospect changes the calculus of motivation considerably; knowing that careful work in July will translate into tangible credit in September, more students will commit themselves to completion. Beginning the year with a respectable grade establishes a cushion against future difficulties, a reservoir of success upon which to draw when November's examinations prove unexpectedly treacherous.

Teachers, of course, recognize that summer constitutes their respite as well—those precious weeks when lesson plans recede and their own lives demand attention. They understand, too, that students scatter during vacation: some to distant relatives, others to camps and beaches, most to the simple pleasure of unstructured days with companions their own age. This shared appreciation for summer's essential character would naturally incline teachers toward assignments both reasonable in scope and perhaps even tinged with enjoyment. Such projects need not burden students with stress or consume entire weeks; they should instead engage the mind without monopolizing time, keeping intellectual faculties gently active rather than allowing them to grow entirely dormant.

Proponents of student-designed projects contend that autonomy breeds investment—that young people, granted freedom to pursue topics of genuine interest, will approach summer work with greater enthusiasm and creativity. This argument possesses surface appeal, yet it founders on a predictable reef: students choosing their own assignments will almost invariably select paths of least resistance, crafting projects so simple they border on trivial.

The case for teacher-designed summer projects thus rests on multiple pillars: they preview forthcoming curriculum, they generate meaningful grades, and they balance intellectual engagement with the season's rightful claim to leisure. Everyone prospers when structure comes not from students themselves but from those who understand both the destination and the journey required to reach it.

The present study extends the foundational work of Lenc and Vedaldi (2015), which demonstrated that convolutional neural network representations at the FC7 layer exhibit a certain degree of equivariance to various classes of transformations, and that training with a particular group of transformations enhances this equivalence property. The authors have undertaken an ambitious experimental program, training upward of thirty networks with different forms of data jitter—an undertaking that commands respect for its scope and thoroughness. Yet the reader searches in vain for a unifying insight, a central thesis that might organize these manifold observations into coherent argument.

To be sure, the authors have examined properties at a layer distinct from that explored by Lenc and Vedaldi, but beyond this modest shift in focus, one finds little that advances our understanding past the well-established principle that jitter augmentation promotes invariance. The evaluation appears largely sound in its execution, yet the paper fails to deliver on the promise implicit in its title, leaving one with the impression of diligent labor that has not quite discovered its purpose.

The most serious difficulties emerge in the experiments concerning representation distances. First, the exclusive focus on FC7 invites skepticism. This layer stands immediately before the final classification layer, FC8, which produces class likelihoods through mere linear projection. Consequently, what the equivalence mapping accomplishes is simply the reprojection of FC8 weights from the attached network onto those of the original network—a transformation more mundane than revelatory. Surely the already-trained networks might yield richer insights if similar experiments were conducted across multiple layers, revealing the architecture's deeper geometry.

Second, the representation distance experiment neglects to report classification error on the testing dataset, an omission that leaves unanswered the fundamental question of whether these representations are indeed compatible up to linear transformation. Without this anchor in predictive performance, the distance metrics float free of practical consequence.

Third, the K-nearest-neighbor experiment suffers from ambiguous specification. Does the measurement occur per test-set example? Is it performed after training the equivalence map? Greater clarity would emerge from demonstrating that networks trained on similar groups of jitter transformations achieve greater compatibility on the target task itself, rather than on some auxiliary metric.

Fourth, the proposed method fails to improve equivariance consistently across all tasks examined. Given that the regularization parameters λ₁ and λ₂ assume such diminutive values, the loss function reduces essentially to simple data jitter, merely summing the losses of original and transformed images. One suspects that the problem lies again in the selection of FC7 as the locus of investigation.

In sum, this paper presents certain intriguing results regarding FC7 equivariance, yet extracts from these experiments disappointingly few novel observations. The deficiencies in the equivalence experiments, combined with the underwhelming results of equivariance fine-tuning, argue against acceptance in the manuscript's present form. Nevertheless, a thoroughgoing refinement of the experiments on already-trained networks, coupled with a restructuring that emphasizes investigative depth over breadth, might yet yield a contribution of genuine interest to the field.

Several minor issues deserve mention as well. The new criterion for equivariance mapping lacks experimental verification of its superiority. Angles cited on pages one and five appear without units—presumably degrees. On page three, where the text observes that "In practice, it is difficult...," the object of maximization or minimization is not the mapping Mᵍ itself but rather the loss function evaluated over Mᵍ. The footnote on page four describes halving activations as dropout, though such constant scaling can be absorbed into adjacent weights, making the terminology questionable. The architecture employed for RVL-CDIP requires clarification: does it match AlexNet's design? Finally, in Figure 3a and 3b on page seven, rendering diagonal elements white proves genuinely misleading, perhaps even erroneous, since the distance between identical representations should register as zero—a property that also serves to verify experimental correctness.
style_literary.coling::1eb3e11f-345c-4e21-9971-65b1c025:
When a school offers its students the possibility of attending classes through online platforms or video conferencing, it creates conditions under which learning may genuinely flourish. In 2009, schools first began providing this program to their surrounding communities. Most families residing in the immediate vicinity regarded the innovation as superfluous, even detrimental; families living at considerable distances, however, recognized in it a stroke of brilliance. The program took its initial form at Generic_School, where approximately ninety-two students participated in that inaugural year. The first year proved successful, as did the second, though this early promise would not endure.

After that second year, the number of participating students began its steady, troubling decline. Why were fewer students drawn to the program as time progressed? What interventions might arrest this erosion of interest? Why did families living nearby dismiss what families living far away embraced? When the program allowing students to attend classes online or through video conferencing commenced at Generic_School on September 2, 2009, ninety-two students enrolled, and all of them expressed satisfaction with the arrangement; yet only seventy percent returned for the following year. In the second year, merely sixty-five students joined the online classes. The comments they submitted revealed a telling ambivalence: "It's pleasant to remain at home and take classes online, and it's wonderful not to worry about arriving late to class, but as a student I've longed to share ideas and thoughts with other students." By the third year of the program's operation, enrollment had plummeted to a mere ten percent of its original figure. From 2011 onward, only about twenty students participated in the online program annually. The numbers dwindled because students discovered that remaining at home throughout the day bred a stifling monotony, a sense of isolation that gnawed at them. Unable to exchange ideas with their peers or engage with them in spontaneous conversation, students recognized that they required more varied activities and less confinement to a single, unchanging location.

Several strategies might rekindle student interest in the program and restore its vitality. Within the online classes themselves, participants could be offered meaningful choices before joining any particular course. These choices might include the option to venture out and collaborate on projects with other students enrolled in the same classes, the ability to communicate through chat interfaces to share information and arrange meetings on mutually convenient days. For those who preferred to avoid in-person gatherings, video chat or voice chat with fellow students could serve as alternatives. Another possibility worth exploring: students could be granted the option to visit the school campus once weekly or once monthly, thereby preserving some thread of physical connection to the institution. If these options prove effective, enrollment will almost certainly increase, drawing more and more students into the fold.

Many residents of the area surrounding Generic_School believed in 2009 that these online classes constituted a wasteful diversion, fearing that opening such alternatives would diminish school attendance precipitously. Several families went so far as to confront the principal directly, declaring: "For many years our goal has been to ensure students attend school regularly, and with this program in place our goal will surely fail." The principal responded with patience and principle: "Certainly, we want as many students as possible to attend school in person, but for various reasons not all of them can reach our campus, and we have decided to offer this program as both a benefit and an opportunity for those who might otherwise be denied an education." The principal convened numerous meetings with parents who harbored reservations about the initiative. After a month of deliberation and discussion, most came to accept and understand the program's essential purpose and underlying philosophy.

Families living at great distances from the school regarded the program as nothing short of inspired, for it meant their children would no longer endure lengthy commutes each day. Money would be saved, hours reclaimed, and a genuine opportunity secured for their children to learn from home in comfort and safety. These distant families, moved by gratitude, organized themselves collectively and made generous donations to the school to support extracurricular activities such as soccer, track, and other athletic endeavors. The school administration understood that they had brought genuine happiness to these families, and that recognition of others' needs had always been their deepest goal: fostering happiness and ensuring that everyone felt comfortable in their pursuit of learning. Schools must vigilantly look out for those who lack the means to travel long distances or who live far from traditional educational institutions. Online and video conferencing classes represent a powerful beginning in the effort to serve the entire community with equity and imagination.

I am grateful for this stimulating contribution to the literature. The information bottleneck principle holds considerable appeal for me, and I welcome its extension into the domain of deep neural networks. To the best of my understanding, this paper represents the first attempt to employ IB in the training of deep architectures—the foundational papers having merely articulated the concept itself—though I note below certain reservations concerning the claim of independent discovery.

The derivation of the variational lower bound unfolds with admirable clarity, accessible even to readers whose acquaintance with variational inference remains modest. The explication of the IB principle, too, achieves a welcome lucidity. The experimental results, insofar as one can judge from the evidence presented, appear genuinely promising and suggest fruitful avenues for further investigation.

The presentation of the model itself, however, strikes me as somewhat perplexing. In the established conventions of variational inference and information maximization, p customarily denotes the model proper, while q represents what might be termed the "inference engine"—a distinction that preserves the independence of inference methodology from modeling procedure. The VIB framework presented here, by contrast, treats p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (approximated through empirical distribution), which entails that the actual model becomes q(y|z)p(z|x). The authors subsequently introduce p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in the second paragraph of section 4.2.3, page 8. Predictive in what sense, precisely? I surmise the intended meaning is p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz, yet this interpretation places the two definitions in apparent contradiction with one another—a tension that wants resolution.

The connection drawn to variational autoencoders and warm-up training (through beta tuning) proves intriguing. Nevertheless, even when the loss function formula coincides exactly with the variational lower bound employed in VAE (where beta equals unity), the underlying models diverge fundamentally. Consider: r(z) in VIB serves as the variational approximation to p(z)—meaning r(z) constitutes no component of the model itself—whereas in VAE it functions as the prior distribution, genuinely defined within the modeling procedure. Similarly, p(z|x) in VIB belongs to the model, while in VAE that same term represents the approximate posterior, subject to independent selection (one might, for instance, implement p(x|z) as a deep neural network while choosing for p(z|x) either another deep network or a Gaussian process).

In sum, the presentation of the modeling procedure lacks the precision one might wish for. I hope these points will receive clearer treatment in revision, as the current exposition leaves me, speaking as someone trained in Bayesian reasoning, with a certain discomfort. Regarding the VAE section, it would strengthen the paper to articulate explicitly the distinctions between VIB and VAE, offering some intuitive justification should the VIB interpretation be preferred.

Minor errors warrant attention: Equations 9-11 appear to employ q(z|y) where q(y|z) was intended; Figure 2's caption references "as beta becomes smaller" where "larger" seems correct.

Concerning the claim of independent work: the authors assert their manuscript developed independently of Chalk et al. 2016, available online since May of that year. Contemporary deep learning research proceeds at such competitive intensity that simultaneous discovery has become commonplace. I am inclined to credit this assertion and commend the authors' forthrightness. Should it prove otherwise, however, I could not recommend acceptance.
style_literary.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper under consideration presents an approach to machine translation training data selection, one that employs a convolutional neural network classifier to score and rank sentences drawn from general-domain corpora. The authors execute their comparison to previous work—work relying on continuous or n-gram-based language models—with admirable thoroughness, though one notes the absence of any explicit comparison against methods of bilingual data selection, such as the sum of cross-entropy differences.

Initially, the motivation for choosing a CNN architecture over the more familiar RNN or LSTM remained opaque to me. Yet this proves, upon reflection, to be among the paper's genuine strengths: the authors argue persuasively that certain segments within a text or sentence carry greater importance than others, and that the convolutional structure captures precisely this selective attention. What the paper fails to demonstrate experimentally, however, is whether bag-of-words representations prove more valuable than sequential ones—or whether some combination of the two yields superior results, and for what reasons.

The textual description of the CNN itself, whether relying on one-hot encodings or semi-supervised learning with pre-trained embeddings, achieves clarity and detail, calling attention to the salient architectural features. Still, a visual diagram of the layers, illustrating how inputs combine and flow through the network, would communicate what a thousand words of prose cannot.

The writing throughout maintains a professional standard, though certain citation parentheses appear unnecessary—the distinction between narrative and parenthetical citation formats, between \citet and \citep, seems to have escaped notice at line 385, for instance.

The experiments and evaluation lend credible support to the paper's central claims, yet I harbor some concern regarding the method by which the authors determine the optimal number of in-domain sentences to select, as described at line 443, which relies on a separate validation set. Several questions arise: What validation data, precisely, do they employ? On what data do they tune the CNN hyperparameters? How sensitive do the models prove to these choices? Furthermore, Table 2 ought properly to compare the various approaches while holding constant the number of sentences selected; Figure 1 suggests, encouragingly, that even under such fair comparison the proposed approach would outperform the baselines.

Additional observations present themselves. I would welcome an experiment comparing this technique against baseline methods when more abundant in-domain data becomes available, not merely the development set. The results or discussion section might profitably include example sentences selected by the different methods, lending concrete support to the claims advanced in section 5.4. Regarding the argument about abstracting away from surface forms: another baseline worth considering would be the work of Axelrod in 2015, who replaced certain words with part-of-speech tags to reduce language model data sparsity—a comparison that would reveal whether word2vec embeddings confer additional advantage.

The summing of source and target classification scores bears striking resemblance to source-and-target Lewis-Moore language model data selection through summed cross-entropy differences; a reference to this work near line 435 would seem appropriate. Finally, one wonders whether the authors might learn optimal weights for combining source and target scores by extending their CNN architecture to the bilingual, parallel setting.
style_literary.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
The present paper unveils Edward, a probabilistic programming language constructed atop the foundations of TensorFlow and Python, its architecture designed to accommodate the most widely adopted methodologies in contemporary probabilistic machine learning across a remarkably broad spectrum.

Regarding quality, the Edward library delivers what can only be characterized as an extraordinarily impressive assemblage of modern probabilistic inference techniques, all packaged in forms readily accessible to practitioners. The authors furnish readers with a concise yet substantive survey of the field's most consequential methods, particularly those arising from representation learning perspectives, this theoretical exposition fortified by two empirical demonstrations: one examining various modern variational inference approaches, the other exploring GPU-accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo implementations.

The first experiment, centered on variational inference, would achieve substantially greater value were the authors to provide explicit, unambiguous links to complete, reproducible code corresponding to the reported results. The HMC experiment appears methodologically sound, save for one troubling characterization: describing Stan as hand-optimised strikes this reader as fundamentally unfair, given that the codebase has manifestly not been hand-tuned for this particular model or hardware configuration. No one seriously questions the implementation's technical merit, so why compromise the presentation's integrity with unsubstantiated, sensationalist assertions? A more illuminating approach would juxtapose Edward against Stan in single-core configurations, then separately document the additional performance gains achieved through parallelisation and GPU acceleration. Such disaggregated metrics would empower readers to extrapolate performance expectations across diverse hardware landscapes.

Concerning clarity, the manuscript generally achieves lucid exposition and maintains readability throughout. The numerous code examples prove helpful, though they simultaneously present difficulties: often what has been omitted remains unclear. The authors would serve their audience well by providing—and prominently linking to—a machine-readable companion document (a Jupyter notebook would prove ideal, though even plain text or HTML would facilitate copy-pasting more effectively than the PDF format constrains).

Regarding originality, the Edward library undeniably constitutes a singular collection of probabilistic inference methodologies. The principal challenge to the paper's novelty emerges from the same research group's previous publications. The manuscript references Tran et al. (2016a), which traverses considerably overlapping territory, albeit from divergent vantage points. Whether that companion paper has secured publication or remains under submission—and if so, in what venue—remains frustratingly unclear.

As for significance, Edward appears positioned to exert profound influence across both Bayesian machine learning and deep learning domains.

Additional observations warrant mention: Section 2 draws sharp distinctions between specialised languages (Stan among them) and Turing-complete languages like Edward. This demarcation seems questionable, as Stan too possesses Turing completeness. Moreover, the authors provide no formal proof establishing Edward's Turing-completeness, leaving this foundational claim unsubstantiated.
style_literary.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
The submission under review pursues a genuinely interesting approach to character-based language modeling — one that preserves word-level representations within the context and, optionally, within the output layer as well. Yet the fundamental architecture cannot be called new. Kim and colleagues developed a closely related framework in 2015, as the authors themselves acknowledge; Jozefowicz and his collaborators extended similar ideas a year later. Both predecessor studies, it must be noted, already surpass the present work in certain respects, having applied their methods using recurrent neural networks and long short-term memory architectures. Jozefowicz's team, moreover, provided a comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling — a synthesis conspicuously absent here. The authors would do well to engage this existing literature more thoroughly, situating their contribution within the broader landscape. What remains as the principal novelty, then, is the application to machine translation, though even here questions linger: to what extent can reranking N-best lists genuinely address the out-of-vocabulary problem? The translation-specific dimensions of this challenge deserve more elaborate treatment than they receive.

Certain claims advanced in the submission strike this reader as somewhat exaggerated. Consider the assertion in Section 2.3 that their approach renders "the notion of vocabulary obsolete" — a bold proclamation that sits uneasily beside the authors' own expressed doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity measures when no explicit output vocabulary exists. Research on arXiv:1609.08144 demonstrates, after all, that modeling especially frequent word forms still contributes meaningfully to performance.

Section 2.3 claims that the objective function requires a finite vocabulary. This statement holds only if we restrict our units to complete word forms. Through subwords and individual characters, however, one can implicitly cover larger, even theoretically infinite vocabularies using the log-likelihood criterion. Though such coverage would require a model architecture different from the one proposed here, the authors should qualify their assertion accordingly.

The deployment of character embeddings for output generation remains insufficiently clarified. The description offered in Section 2.4 lacks the explicitness one would wish for in a technical exposition.

Regarding the configuration of Noise Contrastive Estimation, readers would benefit from understanding how the authors arrived at the specific parameterization described in Section 3.4 — what explorations preceded this choice, what alternatives were considered and dismissed.

Section 4.1 might usefully acknowledge that Kim and colleagues reached similar conclusions regarding the performance of character embeddings at the output layer. The suggestions for improvement they offered deserve discussion here. Section 4.2 overlooks established methods for calculating and interpreting perplexity for unknown words; Shaik's work at IWSLT 2013 provides relevant guidance. Section 4.4 and Table 4 should provide the size of the full training vocabulary for proper context.

Minor points warrant attention as well: page two's bottom requires "input layers" in the plural; Figure 1's fonts prove far too small for comfortable reading; "that we will note WE" should read "denote"; "the parameters estimation" needs either "parameter" singular or a possessive apostrophe; "in factored way" lacks its article; "a n-best list" requires "an"; and Section 4.2's final sentence about adaptive gradient wants both verb and article to achieve grammatical completion.
style_literary.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
Let me begin by observing that this manuscript sprawls across seventeen pages—seventeen full pages, mind you, unburdened by supplementary materials or appendices. While ICLR imposes no formal constraint upon length, one might reasonably expect authors to exercise a certain restraint, to inhabit imaginatively the position of their readers and resist exploiting such latitude without compelling justification. An overage of one or two pages beyond the customary eight-page convention seems defensible; more than doubling that standard, however, strikes me as an imposition verging on the inconsiderate.

As to the substance: The paper introduces what might charitably be termed a synthetic dataset for sequence learning—synthetic because it derives mechanically from MNIST, itself a modest collection of genuine handwritten digit images. Alongside this fabricated benchmark, the authors advance a training regimen for recurrent networks that progresses through sequences of escalating length, a strategy they designate "incremental learning." Their experimental results demonstrate superiority over unscheduled training on this particular dataset; moreover, they claim advantages over several alternative scheduling approaches that might occur to any practitioner. These assertions rest upon ablation studies conducted exclusively within the narrow confines of their proposed benchmark.

My reservations are manifold and substantial.

First, the work exhibits a troubling paucity of genuine novelty. The incremental learning schedule represents not innovation but rather the most obvious recourse when confronting sequential data—an approach already explored thoroughly by Bengio and colleagues in 2015, by Ranzato in that same year, and by numerous others. The sole contribution of any freshness consists of ablation experiments designed to isolate and verify that performance improvements derive from the curriculum itself—hardly a revelatory finding.

Second, and perhaps more damaging, the authors confine their hypothesis to a single dataset of their own construction, artificially generated for the occasion. Why not subject these ideas to the rigors of authentic sequential data? Language modeling presents itself as an obvious proving ground. One suspects the technique falters in such realistic scenarios. Indeed, I harbor considerable confidence that in language modeling tasks—where vocabularies balloon to tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens—any performance gains would evaporate entirely, bearing no resemblance whatsoever to the dramatic seventy-four percent improvement touted here.

Third, I remain unconvinced that this synthetic dataset possesses any genuine value. The world already groans under the weight of sequential datasets drawn from lived reality: textual corpora, speech recordings, financial time series, and myriad other domains. What distinctive contribution this artificial construction offers remains opaque to me. While proliferating datasets need not inherently constitute malpractice, I cannot shake the impression that this benchmark was engineered expressly to validate the proposed methods—a circular endeavor that would have been rendered unnecessary had the authors demonstrated their approach on established, independently motivated datasets.

Finally, the manuscript's excessive length compounds these difficulties. Much of the bloat stems from experiments bearing no discernible relation to the paper's central argument. Section 6.2, for instance, presents findings entirely orthogonal to the narrative arc. The transfer learning investigations of Section 6.4 suffer from the same irrelevance. Had the authors exercised editorial discipline, excising these digressions and testing their methods against genuine benchmarks, they might have produced something approaching a meaningful contribution.
style_literary.coling::108b67b9-1113-4b28-81da-e218ced4:
The structure you choose for your enterprise determines how profits flow and how liability falls—questions whose answers vary dramatically depending on whether you operate as a sole proprietorship, a single-member LLC, a multi-member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Consider the sole proprietorship: here all profits and losses pass directly to you as an individual, and you bear personal liability for every misfortune that befalls the business. A prudent course would be to form an LLC or seek counsel from a business attorney without delay.

The single-member LLC offers a measured improvement: profits and losses still pass through to you personally, yet your liability remains limited to the company's assets alone. You must, however, shoulder the burden of self-employment tax.

In a multi-member LLC, profits and losses are apportioned according to each member's ownership interest in the enterprise. Self-employment tax applies here as well, falling upon each member in turn.

The LLC with "S" election introduces greater sophistication: you pay yourself a reasonable salary, which escapes the grasp of self-employment tax. Remaining profits and losses pass through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholder's percentage interest. Whether distributions trigger taxation depends upon your basis—a matter sufficiently complex that explanation defies simplification, best left to your certified public accountant.

The S Corporation operates identically.

The C Corporation presents a different picture entirely: corporate profits face taxation at the corporate level, and then any dividends distributed to shareholders face taxation again. This double taxation renders the C Corporation structure disadvantageous for small business owners.

An unethical suggestion, offered merely for the sake of completeness: those seeking a lavish lifestyle, entirely tax-free and requiring minimal exertion, might consider founding a non-profit seed-faith megachurch, broadcasting televised appeals, and persuading credulous masses to send money with promises that God will multiply their "seed of faith" tenfold—a scheme as morally bankrupt as it is legally protected.
style_literary.coling::60e5cc06-240c-4ed3-80bd-353d0ba8:
Solar power stands as one of the authentic miracles wrought by modern science. Yet beneath this achievement lurks a single, persistent complication: the technology remains, stubbornly and significantly, more expensive than alternative sources of electrical generation. Were cost no object, solar would represent an unambiguous triumph; but then, the same proposition holds true for every variety of renewable energy we might name.

Advocates frequently observe that installing solar infrastructure costs no more—and sometimes considerably less—than constructing new conventional facilities, whether nuclear reactors or coal-fired stations. This claim possesses genuine merit when examined at the scale of utility companies and regional grids. For the individual householder, however, the comparison collapses into irrelevance: you will not be erecting your own power plant, and therefore you need not trouble yourself with capital expenditures measured in hundreds of millions of dollars.

Consider instead the prosaic arithmetic of residential installation. Calculate what a single panel costs against the kilowatt-hours it can actually produce, averaged across seasons and weather. Perform this calculation honestly, without wishful thinking.

Some voices insist that if only the government invested sufficient funds, one or perhaps two nuclear facilities could be shuttered immediately. This position rests upon several fundamental misconceptions. To begin with, the government already subsidizes solar purchases throughout California in spectacular fashion—the investment is occurring. Furthermore, government agencies do not themselves operate nuclear power stations; private corporations run these facilities, while regulatory bodies merely establish safety parameters and compliance standards. Consider also the economic structure of nuclear generation: the overwhelming costs concentrate in initial construction and eventual waste disposal, not in the daily operation of a functioning plant. To shutter a productive reactor would squander capital rather than conserve it.

Despite these economic realities, I harbor genuine affection for solar technology, and for compelling reasons. It generates electricity at the point of consumption, eliminating transmission losses across hundreds of miles of wire. It produces virtually zero emissions during operation. It runs in perfect silence—a quality I value more than most. Perhaps most elegantly, it delivers maximum output precisely when demand peaks: summer afternoons, when air conditioners strain against the heat.

Indeed, cooling buildings may represent solar power's ideal application. When summer sun beats down mercilessly, the appetite for conditioned air swells proportionally. Rooftop panels simultaneously generate cooling power while shading the structure beneath them—a double benefit.

Yet measured by pure financial calculus, fossil fuels still deliver cheaper electricity.
style_literary.coling::0303abd4-4ede-45e6-94d9-7e4d9969:
The severity of the outcome depends entirely upon which projections one credits, though the worst possibilities are undeniably catastrophic. Projections of global average climate change exist in the literature, though one must remember that the preponderance of this transformation will manifest itself most dramatically near the polar regions and throughout the world's oceans.

What might such warming actually resemble? Consider, as a historical analog, the warmest epoch in Earth's recent geologic past across the last several hundred million years: the Cretaceous Period. During that extended interval, spanning roughly one hundred to sixty-five million years before our present moment, atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations hovered near one thousand parts per million, while global temperatures exceeded today's averages by approximately ten degrees Celsius. Emissions trajectories and corresponding temperature shifts that begin to approach these ancient conditions remain well within the realm of possibility by the close of the coming century, although reasonable observers continue to debate the actual likelihood of such an extreme scenario materializing.

During the Cretaceous, sea levels stood hundreds of meters higher than those we know today. Central North America lay submerged beneath a shallow inland sea that stretched across the continent's midsection. Deciduous forests flourished in polar latitudes. The elevated temperatures also dramatically intensified both the frequency and destructive power of severe weather phenomena: hurricanes, typhoons, and their devastating cousins.

Under comparable future conditions, most tropical regions would become uninhabitable, or at minimum extremely unpleasant, owing to the combined assault of heat and oppressive humidity. Vast portions of currently inhabited land would lie completely underwater, displacing hundreds of millions, perhaps billions, of human beings. Freshwater resources would grow increasingly scarce as every glacial source melted away entirely. Meanwhile, the northern reaches of the Canadian wilderness would acquire climates reminiscent of the Mediterranean basin.

This accounting does not yet address the profound alterations in ocean salinity and acidity, transformations that would precipitate mass extinctions of marine life—a critical protein source for human populations—nor the disappearance of countless terrestrial species unable to migrate or adapt with sufficient speed to their shifting habitats and ranges.
style_literary.coling::564547e8-c996-4ee6-8beb-abfe8062:
The energy unleashed by a clap remains constant regardless of location; what shifts is the destination of that energy. Consider a terrestrial clap: the collision's energy disperses through several channels. First, sound. Second, the deformation of your hands. Third, heat. Fourth, various minor losses that likely remain consistent across different environments and need not concern us here.

Let us construct a rudimentary model of the clap itself. Two hands, each weighing five hundred grams, approaching one another at two meters per second. Since energy equals mass times velocity squared, we arrive at roughly four joules.

Though we might classify a clap as an elastic collision, some small fraction of energy inevitably vanishes into deformation. Microscopic examination would doubtless reveal cellular damage, though minimal. The voracious consumer of energy, however, proves to be heat. Research indicates that a clap lasts approximately twenty milliseconds—a crude estimate, certainly—while comparative data on sound power suggests that an alarm clock provides a reasonable analogue. Even should our calculations err by a factor of one hundred, the conclusion holds. Through the roughest, most unrefined integration of the sound wave's duration with the power output, we derive a total acoustic energy of two millionths of a joule per clap. Set against the four joules entering the collision on Earth, sound accounts for a mere five hundred-thousandths of one percent of the total energy released. The remainder transforms into heat and deformation, though I would not hazard even the crudest guess at their respective proportions.

Thus, to address the question directly: on Earth, only 0.00005 percent of a clap's energy manifests as sound. The remainder dissipates as heat and hand deformation. In space, zero percent becomes sound, and that infinitesimal fraction that would have propagated acoustically on Earth simply converts to additional thermal energy instead. The sonic component of a clap carries such negligible energy compared to the heat generated by the initial collision that the interaction remains essentially unchanged—save for the absence of any audible report. The silence, in other words, costs almost nothing.
style_literary.coling::31049c2c-a6a8-44a9-acaa-b8e3b123:
The phenomenon turns on two axes: anonymity and vulnerability.

In digital space, you speak from behind a veil, and the body of your interlocutor remains safely beyond arm's reach. This geometric fact transforms disagreement into something sharper, more naked in its hostility—because aggression costs nothing when no fist can answer it. One may bark with impunity across the unbridgeable distance.

Consider the physical world and its older calculus. If you stand five feet tall and weigh ninety pounds dripping wet, you will likely swallow your opinion when facing a man six-foot-five and two hundred fifty pounds, even if you believe him utterly wrong. But online? The threat dissolves. What, precisely, can he do?

The reciprocal truth proves equally significant. Cruelty comes easier when your target exists only as typography on a screen, a username divorced from flesh. The medium itself strips away humanity, reducing the other to pure text, to abstraction.

Thus: watching a mediocre YouTube video, you type effortlessly that xXUsernameXx is a talentless piece of shit. The words flow without friction. But imagine now the translation into embodied space—walking up to Jenny, the fourteen-year-old girl who records Minecraft videos to forget her parents' divorce, meeting her eyes directly, and speaking those same words aloud: "You're a talentless piece of shit." The sentence catches in your throat. The child's face makes speech impossible.

What of automobiles? The same architecture applies. You sit encased in a locked metal shell that functions as half armor, half escape pod. You lean on your horn, raise your middle finger freely, because this intersection marks both your turn and your last glimpse of that driver. And fuck that fucking stupid fucking Ford that cut you off—because it remains merely a Ford, an object, not Jenny's mother navigating a terrible day, her mind circling obsessively around rent she cannot pay, her attention fractured by financial terror.
style_literary.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1:
Long before infants command what we properly call language, they shape their first utterances through babble—an exploratory play with sound itself, produced by the simplest alternation of open and closed mouths. These earliest vocalizations emerge because they represent the path of least resistance for a developing child's articulatory apparatus. Consider the mechanics as a kind of binary system: zero designates the open vowel sound, that unobstructed "aaaaaa"; one marks the closed consonant, the sealed lips forming "m" or "p." Attempt this yourself. Press your lips together as though beginning "m" or "p," then simply release them while expelling air—what emerges is essentially "ma" or "pa." The consonants "b," "d," and "p" function almost interchangeably in this closed position, which explains the universal variations: baba, abba, papa, dada, and their endless permutations. These constitute the fundamental architecture of human vocalization, and so naturally they become the infant's preferred instruments—the mouth's most economical gestures.

What proves particularly fascinating is how these pre-linguistic children have, in effect, given birth to language itself through the naming of mother and father. Why did adult speakers across cultures accept and perpetuate this infant nomenclature? Perhaps the widespread designation of bodily functions—"poo" and "wee" in English and their cognates elsewhere—follows a similar logic of articulatory simplicity. Grandparents, too, receive labels constructed from these same binary elements in numerous languages. Hindi offers an elegant demonstration: Paternal Grandfather becomes दादा (daadaa), Paternal Grandmother becomes दादी (daadii), Maternal Grandfather becomes नाना (naanaa), Maternal Grandmother becomes नानी (naanii). Each term builds itself from that primal alternation of closed and open, consonant and vowel, as though language itself remembers its origins in the mouth of a child discovering that air, tongue, and lips can conjure meaning from pure sound, that the body itself can become an instrument of connection and address.
style_literary.coling::ef4cca12-c45c-4b1b-9c67-8db766ad:
Imagine yourself a merchant in seventeenth-century Amsterdam, and imagine further that among the city's wealthiest women there exists an insatiable appetite for cumin—the spice, that is, not some passing curiosity but a genuine passion. The difficulty, of course, lies in the fact that cumin grows nowhere within a thousand miles of Amsterdam's canals and gabled houses; one must venture to the distant markets of the Middle East or the subcontinent of India to procure this precious commodity, and the journey transforms what is elsewhere abundant into something extravagantly dear. There, in those far-off lands, cumin flourishes with the persistence of common weeds and commands prices that would make an Amsterdam housewife laugh. Could you but transport that inexpensive Eastern cumin to your Northern city, fortunes would be yours for the taking.

The obstacle, however, proves formidable: the only feasible method requires dispatching a substantial vessel on a voyage lasting nine months or more. This enterprise demands enormous capital—a seaworthy ship must be acquired, a competent captain secured, a full crew hired, all requiring wages for the better part of a year—and beyond the expense looms the specter of catastrophic risk. Ships founder in storms, cargoes spoil in holds, and the ocean keeps its own counsel regarding which ventures it will permit to succeed.

How, then, does one accomplish such an undertaking? Unless you possess stupendous wealth yourself—and precious few individuals or organizations, save perhaps entire nations, command such resources—how do you finance this precarious expedition? You might approach a bank or money-lender for a loan, true enough, but such loans carry interest rates so steep they would devour nearly all potential profits, assuming profits materialized at all. And should the ship sink beneath the waves? Bankruptcy would follow as surely as night follows day, and you would find yourself in debtors' prison, if the money-lender's rougher forms of persuasion had not already found you.

Yet consider an alternative arrangement. You cannot finance this voyage alone, but you could manage, without undue strain, perhaps one-tenth of the total cost. And there, remarkably, you count nine friends, each of whom could similarly afford one-tenth. Together, you forge an agreement: each participant finances a portion of the expedition's cost—in effect, each "purchases stock" in the enterprise—receiving shares representing one-tenth of the whole. With this pooled capital, you commission the vessel, hire the crew, and send them forth. Nine months hence, the ship returns, its hold laden with fragrant, costly cumin. The profits exceed the initial investment handsomely, and each investor receives one-tenth of those considerable returns.

But what transpires should the vessel sink? Well, it remains a genuine misfortune, certainly—particularly for the crew, whose loss transcends the merely financial—but you have risked only one-tenth of the cost, a sum you can absorb without ruin, without facing the money-lender's vengeance. Because the risk has been distributed among ten parties, no single individual faces debtors' prison. Everyone sustains a modest loss rather than one person suffering complete devastation.

Contemplate this arrangement and all who participate in it. The fashionable ladies obtain their cumin, and at prices lower than they might otherwise pay. The shipwrights find employment constructing a new vessel. The captain and crew secure work and wages. The Indian trader gains a fresh customer for his goods. And naturally, you and your associates grow wealthy in the bargain. In short, every single participant finds themselves better off than before, and none of this would have materialized without this concept of buying and selling stocks.

Herein lies the advantage of a stock market: it channels capital from places where it sits idle and inert to places where it can be deployed productively, and in the process, general prosperity increases. It distributes risk across numerous participants, liberating individuals from the paralyzing fear of total ruin.

Now, admittedly, the modern American stock market suffers from certain pathologies. The valid critique holds that it has ceased performing its proper function—namely, allocating capital toward productive uses—and has transformed from means into end, from instrument into idol. Nevertheless, the fundamental concept of a stock market remains brilliant, and only the most doctrinaire communist could oppose it in principle. This mechanism has given us railroads and automobiles, computers and telephones, abundant food and effective medicines—all the modern conveniences we consider indispensable to civilized life.
style_literary.coling::97ce3bac-5618-4fcb-8600-bcf08ed8:
Let me be candid: unless you possess considerable experience with wines, confronting two similar bottles on a merchant's shelf, you will almost certainly fail to divine which vintage will better please your palate. What lies within your grasp, however, is the more modest but achievable task of determining which broad categories of wine appeal to your particular taste. To accomplish even this limited goal, you must actually sample a representative selection of different wines—a process that, regrettably, demands some financial outlay. Furthermore, should you happen to be merely five years old, purchasing wine in the United States remains strictly prohibited by law, rendering the entire enterprise moot.

Wines are customarily classified according to two primary criteria: the geographic origin of their grapes and the particular species from which those grapes derive, a designation the trade calls the wine's "varietal." Among red wines, the common varietals include Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah—which occasionally travels under the name Shiraz—and Zinfandel. The white wines offer their own roster: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, sometimes labeled Pinot Grigio, along with Riesling and the distinctively aromatic Gewürztraminer.

When tasting wines, attend closely to the specific qualities that give you pleasure. Consider, for instance, that many red wines possess a characteristic flavor that leaves the mouth feeling parched, almost dusty. This sensation, known in the wine world as a "tannic" quality, arises from organic molecules called tannins. Should you discover that you enjoy this astringent character, a notably tannic varietal such as Cabernet Sauvignon might prove well suited to your preferences. Among white wines, the most readily perceptible characteristics include acidity—which is to say, sourness—and residual sugar content, qualities that require little elaborate explanation to identify. Another trait worth noting in both red and white wines is what connoisseurs term "oakiness." When you detect a wood-like aroma emanating from the glass, you have encountered this particular flavor profile.

Throughout this exploration, bear in mind an essential truth: no such thing as a universally superior wine exists. What matters entirely is which type you personally prefer, even should that preference lead you to select a ten-dollar jug over a five-hundred-dollar bottle of distinguished Bordeaux Cabernet. Moreover, when uncertainty clouds your judgment, do not hesitate to solicit guidance from the waiter, the sommelier, or the wine shop employee. These professionals, given even the vaguest notion of your desires, can typically direct you toward something that will satisfy your taste while respecting your budgetary constraints. Their expertise exists precisely to navigate such dilemmas.

Alexander's triumph at Issus rests upon several interlocking factors, each deserving careful examination. The matter of numerical superiority requires immediate revision: modern scholarship has thoroughly discredited Arrian's improbable figure of six hundred thousand Persian troops. Hans Delbrück, considering the formidable logistical obstacles inherent in provisioning and maneuvering such multitudes in ancient warfare, proposes a force as modest as twenty-five thousand. Most historians, including Engels and Green, settle upon a Persian strength not exceeding one hundred thousand at Issus—a total comprising eleven thousand cavalry, ten thousand of the famed Immortals, and ten thousand Greek mercenaries. Warry's estimate reaches one hundred eight thousand. These reassessments fundamentally alter our understanding of the engagement's scale and character.

Moreover, the Macedonians possessed superior armament and training when measured against ordinary Persian infantry, finding their equals only among Darius's Greek hirelings. Though outnumbered, Alexander faced an adversary heavily weighted toward lightly-armed peltasts rather than solid infantry capable of sustained close combat. Consequently, the two armies fielded roughly equivalent numbers of heavy foot soldiers, the decisive element in pitched battle.

The Companion cavalry, that instrument of Macedonian dominance, represented the finest mounted arm then existing—against them, Persian horsemen could offer no credible resistance. Alexander wielded these horsemen with devastating precision, executing the hammer-and-anvil maneuver with ruthless efficiency. This quintessential shock tactic operates through brutal simplicity: one force pins the enemy in place while another crashes into their vulnerable flank or rear, producing catastrophic physical destruction and psychological disintegration simultaneously. Its effectiveness transcends mere casualties inflicted during the fighting itself, for the greatest slaughter in ancient warfare invariably occurred during rout and pursuit, when broken formations dissolved into panicked flight. Here emerges the fundamental truth that numbers, however impressive, cannot substitute for discipline—that quality which distinguishes armies from armed mobs and which the Macedonian phalanx possessed in unsurpassed measure.
