Among the arsenal of cybersecurity defenses available to network administrators, the Intrusion Detection System stands as an essential sentinel, identifying malicious traffic and discerning the signatures of cyberattacks before they can inflict damage. In recent years, buoyed by the spectacular successes of machine learning — particularly deep learning — more and more of these detection systems have come to rely upon algorithmic intelligence, accelerating the speed with which they recognize threats. Yet for all their computational sophistication, these systems betray a troubling brittleness: they falter when confronted by attack patterns they have never encountered before. As new threats proliferate — especially those targeting the sprawling, vulnerable networks of Internet of Things devices — the need for a more resilient detection system, one capable of recognizing the unusual and the unprecedented, grows urgent.

This work explores whether generative adversarial models might fortify the robustness of machine learning-based intrusion detection. We propose a novel method, which we call SIGMA, that harnesses adversarial examples to strengthen these systems against unfamiliar attack types. Employing Generative Adversarial Networks in concert with metaheuristic algorithms, SIGMA generates adversarial instances iteratively, using them to retrain the detection system until the rate of successful detection converges — that is, until no further improvement can be wrung from the process. Each round of enhancement unfolds in three phases: a generative phase, during which GANs and metaheuristics produce synthetic attack instances; an evaluation phase, in which we measure how many of these newly minted threats the system successfully detects; and finally a training phase, wherein the detector learns from these adversarial examples. We tested SIGMA across four standard machine learning classification algorithms, pairing GAN architecture with a hybrid genetic and local-search algorithm to synthesize new attack datasets. Our results demonstrate that SIGMA successfully generates adversarial attacks against diverse machine learning-based systems, improving detection performance up to one hundred percent after merely two iterative rounds.
style_literary.coling::f249dac3-f3a2-4db9-9758-e18c9f8f:
Consider a town where residents crowd into apartments, some harboring dreams of house ownership. The builders, sensing this yearning, respond by erecting homes throughout the neighborhood. When these properties reach the market, demand proves intense—buyers outnumber available houses, and competition among purchasers drives prices steadily upward. This reverses the familiar dynamic where competition among sellers moderates cost; here, scarcity empowers those who control supply.

A wave of buyers acquires houses at these inflated prices, and valuations continue their ascent while desire remains robust. Eventually, however, the market reaches a threshold: prices climb beyond what newcomers will pay, or the pool of aspiring homeowners exhausts itself, each household having secured its dwelling. Demand collapses with startling suddenness, and the cost of houses begins falling.

Those who purchased near the peak now confront a bitter arithmetic—they have paid premium prices for depreciating assets. Seeking to stanch their losses, many resolve to return to apartment life and divest themselves of their houses. This exodus floods the market with properties, transforming scarcity into abundance, and prices plummet with gathering velocity. The descent continues until valuations reach a point where equilibrium reasserts itself, stabilizing at levels far below the previous heights.

The anatomy of a bubble reveals itself in this pattern: a market characterized by constrained supply and voracious demand metamorphoses, often abruptly, into one glutted with supply yet starved of buyers. The phenomenon proves self-reinforcing in both directions. During the ascent, rising prices lure investors hoping to capitalize on continued appreciation, intensifying competition and accelerating the climb. During the collapse, falling prices prompt holders to flee, each sale adding to the surplus and deepening the downturn. The market becomes a mechanism that amplifies its own extremes, carrying participants toward unsustainable heights before casting them into equally unsustainable depths. Understanding this cyclical nature illuminates why bubbles form with such regularity throughout economic history.
style_literary.coling::7a09dbe7-814b-4d82-b5b3-a15b926a: The difficulty lies in their resistance to assimilation. In earlier centuries, they lived as nomads, traversing continents in an endless migration that carried them through countless cities and settlements. Wherever they paused, even briefly, certain losses occurred—animals vanished, produce disappeared—yet because they possessed genuine skill in various crafts and trades, and because they inevitably moved on, the settled populations tolerated these minor depredations without excessive complaint. Then came the communist regime, which brought this ancient pattern to an abrupt halt, for the new order forbade freedom of movement as a matter of policy. The method of enforcement was brutally simple and devastatingly effective: authorities confiscated their horses outright and physically removed the wheels from their caravans and wagons. Thus, in what seemed scarcely more than a single night, an entire way of life that had persisted for generations was rendered impossible, and they were compelled to abandon everything they had known and attempt to forge a completely different existence. This catastrophic rupture has led inexorably to the present circumstances. Many now subsist parasitically upon our social welfare systems, and whenever they encounter refusal or even a skeptical glance, whenever they are discovered in some illegal activity, they immediately invoke accusations of racial discrimination. Education, generally speaking, holds little value in their culture, and those among them who do pursue learning and adopt conventional lifestyles are often regarded within their own communities as traitors to their heritage and ancestral traditions. Then there is the criminal element, which cannot be ignored. Pickpocketing is common, shoplifting from markets routine, fraudulent claims for state benefits widespread. The largest and most powerful criminal organization in our entire nation is, in fact, an extended gypsy clan with connections to virtually every illicit enterprise imaginable: narcotics trafficking, contract violence, human smuggling, prostitution rings, illegal weapons trade. The statistical reality remains stark: one is far more likely to encounter a gypsy engaged in antisocial or criminal behavior than one living productively and peacefully. This situation shows no signs of improvement, particularly because those who genuinely wish to integrate and live as ordinary citizens continue to face contempt and ostracism from their own people.

Phylogenetic networks — those leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs employed to capture evolutionary histories that refuse to conform to treelike patterns — stand as generalizations of their simpler cousins, phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number, a quantity of central importance, emerges from a precise arithmetic: one sums the indegrees across all nodes, subtracts the total count of nodes, then adds one. Thus formulated, the Hybridization Number problem presents itself: given a collection of phylogenetic trees as input, one must construct a network that embeds each tree while minimizing this hybridization number.

We present an algorithm addressing this problem for three binary phylogenetic trees labeled on n leaves, achieving a running time of O(c^k poly(n)), where k denotes the hybridization number of an optimal network and c represents some positive constant. For the simpler case involving only two trees, researchers had previously proposed an algorithm running in time O(3.18^k n), yet an algorithm with running time O(c^k poly(n)) for more than two trees had, prior to this investigation, remained frustratingly elusive. The two-tree algorithm exploits the intimate connection to acyclic agreement forests, thereby achieving a linear exponent in its running time, while previous approaches to problems involving more than two trees — whether explicitly or implicitly — relied upon brute force enumeration through all conceivable underlying network topologies, yielding running times that cannot be expressed as O(c^k poly(n)) for any constant c.

The connection to acyclic agreement forests grows considerably weaker when one considers more than two trees; consequently, even when the correct agreement forest presents itself, reconstructing the network poses formidable challenges. We establish novel structural results that permit network reconstruction without requiring one to guess the underlying topology beforehand. Our techniques extend naturally to cases involving more than three input trees, with one crucial exception: a key lemma that maps nodes in the network to corresponding tree nodes, thereby minimizing the guesswork inherent in network construction. The principal open problem, therefore, remains the task of proving results that establish such mappings for collections exceeding three trees — a question whose resolution would represent genuine progress in this domain.

At high transmission speeds, the conception of signals as purely digital phenomena within a wire collapses under scrutiny. One must instead envision them as analog waveforms, subject to the physical constraints of matter and time. The transition from one to zero occurs not instantaneously but across a measurable interval, and the signal itself requires time to propagate through the cable's length. Within a Category 5 cable, electromagnetic pulses travel at approximately 0.64 times the speed of light—which translates to roughly 4.8 to 5.3 nanoseconds per meter.

Consider the mathematics of 100-megabit Ethernet: one hundred million bits per second yields one hundred bits within a thousand nanoseconds, or precisely one bit every ten nanoseconds. If the cable extends beyond two meters, multiple bits exist simultaneously within its copper pathways. At the standard maximum length of one hundred meters, fifty distinct bits inhabit the cable at any given moment. The signal cannot possibly maintain uniformity throughout such a distance. In practice, encoding schemes elevate the actual bitrate still higher, compounding this phenomenon.

Visual representations of these signals prove illuminating. A typical 100-megabit Ethernet waveform, when captured and displayed, reveals its fundamentally analog character—rising and falling edges that curve rather than snap into position. Eye diagrams, which superimpose numerous signal transitions upon one another, demonstrate the challenge with particular clarity. The receiver must distinguish whether the voltage resides at the top, middle, or bottom positions—those regions where the black gaps appear in the visualization. The signal proves noisy, and the "eyes" themselves remain distressingly small. As these apertures narrow, detection becomes increasingly difficult; should they disappear entirely, communication fails.

Once this analog, noise-susceptible reality becomes apparent, the necessity for cables engineered to precise specifications grows self-evident. Signal propagation depends upon the spacing between conductors, wire gauge, dielectric materials, and numerous other factors. Interference arrives from both external sources and adjacent wire pairs, which explains why the pairs must be twisted at differing rates relative to one another—a design that minimizes crosstalk through geometric variation.

Standards emerge from this technical necessity. To ensure compatibility between cable and hardware, manufacturers must adhere to known, tested parameters. Yet with sufficient understanding, signals can traverse unconventional media. One remarkable demonstration employed barbed wire as the transmission medium. The configuration matters enormously: the two wires forming each barbed segment run close together and parallel, while the pairs themselves maintain substantial separation from one another. Analysis suggests that barbed wire arranged in this particular geometry affects signal propagation in ways remarkably similar to Category 5 cable. Had the wires within each pair been positioned non-parallel, or had the pairs been spaced too closely, transmission would have failed entirely.

The lesson persists across all implementations: high-speed data transmission remains an analog art masquerading as digital certainty, governed by electromagnetic physics rather than abstract logic, demanding careful attention to geometry, materials, and the stubborn limitations of propagation velocity through imperfect media.

We introduce what we call the binary value principle—a straightforward subset-sum instance expressing the elementary fact that a natural number, when written in binary notation, cannot assume a negative value—and we relate this principle to central problems spanning both proof complexity and algebraic complexity theory. Building upon a well-known hypothesis formulated by Shub and Smale concerning the computational hardness of calculating factorials, we prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the refutation size within the Ideal Proof System (IPS), that powerful algebraic proof system originally introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Conversely, we demonstrate that short IPS refutations of this particular instance serve to bridge the gap separating sufficiently strong algebraic proof systems from their semi-algebraic counterparts. Our results extend to the full-fledged IPS framework a paradigm that Forbes and his collaborators had previously introduced, whereby lower bounds against restricted subsystems of IPS were obtained through the application of restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds; moreover, our work demonstrates that the binary value principle captures precisely the advantage that semi-algebraic reasoning holds over purely algebraic reasoning, at least when the systems involved are sufficiently strong.

Specifically, we establish the following results. First, regarding conditional IPS lower bounds: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals, this principle being defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation summing from i equals one to n of two raised to the power negative i times x sub i, minus one, where the variables x sub i are constrained to be boolean. Furthermore, the related conjecture implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant formulation of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS itself, nor indeed for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems such as Frege. Though simple in its formulation, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of any boolean formula; hence, similar to other results concerning algebraic proofs—Razborov's work, for instance—IPS lower bounds established for this principle do not necessarily entail corresponding lower bounds for Frege or its subsystems.

Second, concerning the relationship between algebraic and semi-algebraic proofs: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle proves necessary for any algebraic proof system to simulate fully any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems this condition is also sufficient. In particular, we introduce an exceptionally strong proof system simulating all known semi-algebraic proof systems, as well as most other known concrete propositional proof systems, under the designation Cone Proof System (CPS), conceived as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system: CPS establishes the unsatisfiability of collections comprising polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals by representing sum-of-squares proofs, along with their extensions, as algebraic circuits. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS if and only if IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle, specifically for the language of systems of equations possessing no zero-one solutions, over both the integers and the rationals.

We turn our attention to a particular challenge in the architecture of distributed storage systems: the design of [ n , k ] linear codes equipped with what is known as the (r , t) - Local Repair Property. Under this property, any collection of t simultaneously failed nodes — where t assumes a value less than or equal to the difference between n and k — can be restored through local repair operations, each node requiring contact with no more than r neighboring nodes. The governing parameters n , k , r , t are positive integers constrained by the relations r less than k less than or equal to n and t less than or equal to n minus k. Our framework assumes two conditions: first, the functional repair model, which permits each repaired node to store not an identical replica of the vanished data but rather a transformed symbol that preserves the (r , t) -local repair property; second, the sequential approach to restoration, wherein the t replacement nodes are arranged in a deliberate order such that each successive newcomer draws its repair information from the surviving nodes and from those newcomers already repaired before it in the sequence. Codes satisfying these criteria — which we designate as (n , k , r , t) -functional locally repairable codes, or FLRCs — constitute the broadest class of locally repairable codes yet formulated, encompassing as special cases several families of codes previously reported in the literature.

The central objective of this investigation is to optimize the storage overhead, or equivalently, to maximize the code rate, achievable by FLRCs. We establish a lower bound on the code length n for the cases where t belongs to the set {2 , 3 } and for arbitrary values of k and r. When t equals 2, our bound extends and generalizes the rate bound demonstrated in earlier work. When t equals 3, our bound sharpens and improves upon the previously established rate bound. Furthermore, we present explicit constructions of exact locally repairable codes for t in {2 , 3 } whose length n attains the derived bound for (n , k , r , t) -FLRCs, thereby confirming the tightness of our theoretical limits and revealing, perhaps surprisingly, that no gap separates the optimal code lengths achievable by functional and exact repair for certain parameter configurations. Finally, our constructions operate over the binary field, rendering them particularly valuable for practical implementation.

Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings occupy a position of considerable importance across multiple domains of machine learning. While this paper centers its attention on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as its primary application, the methods developed here extend naturally to data mining, manifold learning, and related endeavors. Spectral embedding furnishes a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold, thereby rendering the subsequent task—whether clustering with k-means or any of its various approximations—substantially more tractable. Yet despite this reduction in dimensionality, the overall computational burden may remain prohibitively severe for large data sets, owing to two principal factors. First, computing even a partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically demands a Krylov subspace of considerable size. Second, after the spectral embedding stands complete, one must still contend with the same number of data points, a circumstance that may undermine the efficiency of the entire approach. Consider, for instance, that clustering the embedded data proceeds typically through various relaxations of k-means, algorithms whose computational cost scales unfavorably with the size of the data set. Moreover, these methods grow increasingly susceptible to entrapment in local minima, their robustness hinging precariously upon the choice of initial guess.

In this work, we redirect our focus from the entire data set toward a subset of graph vertices—what we term the target subset. We develop two novel algorithms for constructing such a low-dimensional representation of the original graph, one that preserves essential global distances between nodes belonging to the target subset. In particular, this framework permits us to ensure that clustering performed on the target subset remains consistent with the spectral clustering one would obtain from the full data set, were such an undertaking feasible. That consistency emerges through a properly parametrized reduced-order model of the graph-Laplacian, one that approximates with fidelity the diffusion transfer function of the original graph when inputs and outputs are restricted to the target subset. Working with a compact target subset diminishes dramatically the required dimension of the Krylov subspace and allows us to exploit conventional algorithms—approximations of k-means among them—precisely in those regimes where they prove most robust and efficient. Numerical clustering experiments conducted with both synthetic and real-world data have verified these advantages. We note further that our reduced-order modeling approach can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven manner, rendering it the sole feasible option for extremely large graphs not directly accessible to conventional analysis.

Several uses recommend our algorithms. First, they may be employed independently for representative subset clustering in cases where handling the full graph proves either infeasible or simply unnecessary. Second, they serve admirably for quality control. Third, because they reduce the problem size so drastically, they enable the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task at hand—more powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming rather than the conventional Lloyd's algorithm, for example. Finally, they can function as building blocks within a multi-level divide-and-conquer algorithm designed to handle the full graph, a development we shall report in a subsequent article.

Consider the problem of simultaneous localization and mapping — SLAM, in the technical argot — wherein a mobile agent must at once construct a chart of its surroundings and determine its own position within that emerging geography. Dense SLAM algorithms undertake this dual labor at the finest grain: pixel by pixel, they reconstruct space while threading the agent through it. Such precision exacts a steep computational price, one that has long barred these methods from resource-starved, low-power machines.

Approximation offers a path forward. If certain calculations can be loosened without derailing navigation, the agent moves faster, burns less energy. Earlier investigations into approximation assumed the agent's entire trajectory known beforehand — a luxury permitting offline controllers to fix their dials once, at departure, and never touch them again. Reality rarely affords such foreknowledge. When the route unfolds unpredictably, and when those dials may be adjusted in flight, fresh possibilities for conservation emerge.

We present SLAMBooster: an application-aware, online control system governing approximation within dense SLAM as the agent travels. At its core lies the proportional-integral-derivative controller, that workhorse of feedback regulation. Yet our trials revealed a shortcoming. This application-agnostic mechanism, blind to the particular demands of localization, permitted accuracy to deteriorate beyond acceptable limits. SLAMBooster therefore incorporates domain intelligence — smooth surface detection, pose correction — so that approximation bows to navigational imperatives rather than defying them.

Implemented within the open-source SLAMBench framework, SLAMBooster has been tested across more than a dozen trajectories drawn from published datasets and our own fieldwork. The results prove compelling: computation time falls by seventy-two percent on average, energy consumption by thirty-five percent on embedded platforms, all while localization accuracy remains within tolerable margins. These gains are not trivial refinements. They represent the difference between algorithms confined to well-provisioned hardware and algorithms liberated to inhabit a broader ecology of devices, modest in power yet ambitious in purpose.
style_literary.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa: Though the Commission holds a monopoly over the initiation of legislation, both the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union wield powers of amendment and veto as proposed laws wind their way through the labyrinthine corridors of the legislative process. The Treaty on European Union, in its articles nine and ten, declares that the Union observes "the principle of equality of its citizens" and stands founded upon "representative democracy." Yet in practice, these lofty principles of equality and democracy reveal themselves as deficient: the elected representatives seated in Parliament cannot initiate legislation contrary to the Commission's wishes; citizens of the smallest countries command ten times the voting weight in Parliament as their counterparts in the largest countries; and "qualified majorities" or consensus within the Council stand as prerequisites to any act of legislation. The justification offered for this "democratic deficit" embedded within the Treaties has generally been understood to rest upon the notion that complete integration of the European economy and political institutions demanded the technical coordination of experts, even as popular understanding of the Union's purposes developed slowly and nationalist sentiments subsided in the aftermath of war. Over the decades, this arrangement has meant that Parliament gradually assumed greater voice: evolving from an unelected assembly to holding its first direct elections in nineteen seventy-nine, then acquiring increasingly substantial rights within the legislative process itself. Citizens' rights therefore remain limited when measured against the democratic polities flourishing within all European member states: under article eleven of the Treaty on European Union, citizens and associations possess such rights as publicizing their views and submitting an initiative that must receive the Commission's consideration should it gather one million signatures. Article two hundred twenty-seven of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union contains a further right enabling citizens to petition Parliament on issues touching their interests. Parliamentary elections occur every five years, and votes cast for Members of the European Parliament in member states must be organized through proportional representation or a single transferable vote. Seven hundred fifty MEPs sit in session, their numbers allocated in "degressively proportional" fashion according to member state size. This arrangement means that—although the Council ostensibly serves as the body representing member states—within Parliament itself, citizens of smaller member states possess amplified voice compared to citizens dwelling in larger member states. MEPs divide themselves, much as representatives do in national Parliaments, along political party lines: the conservative European People's Party currently holds the largest contingent, while the Party of European Socialists leads the opposition. Parties receive no public funds from the Union, as the Court of Justice held in the matter of Parti écologiste "Les Verts" versus Parliament, ruling that this remained entirely an issue for regulation by the member states. Parliament's powers encompass calling inquiries into maladministration and appointing an Ombudsman pending any court proceedings. It can require that the Commission respond to questions, and by a two-thirds majority can censure the whole Commission, as occurred with the Santer Commission in nineteen ninety-nine. In certain cases, Parliament holds explicit consultation rights, which the Commission must genuinely honor. Nevertheless, its participation in the legislative process remains circumscribed, because no member can actually initiate or pass legislation without both Commission and Council, meaning that power—kratia—does not rest in the hands of directly elected representatives of the people—demos: within the Union, it remains untrue that "the administration is in the hands of the many and not of the few."

Though Martin Luther unleashed fierce polemical storms against his Roman Catholic adversaries on matters touching Mary and the saints, scholars find themselves in broad agreement that the reformer remained faithful to the Marian pronouncements of the ecumenical councils and to the established dogmas of the church. He clung steadfastly to the conviction that Mary was ever-virgin and rightly bore the ancient title Theotokos—Mother of God. Particular scholarly attention falls upon the claim that Luther, some three centuries before Pope Pius IX solemnly defined the Immaculate Conception in 1854, held firmly to that doctrine. Other voices contend that in his later years Luther shifted his stance on the Immaculate Conception—a teaching then undefined within the Church—while maintaining nonetheless Mary's sinlessness throughout the whole course of her earthly life. In Luther's youth, the Assumption of Mary stood as an accepted fact; in time, however, he came to declare that Scripture remained silent on the matter and ceased observing its feast day. Central to his thought was the conviction that Mary and all the saints continue in life beyond death's threshold.

Throughout his long career as priest, professor, and reformer, Luther preached, taught, and disputed about the veneration of Mary with a verbal energy that ranged from the piety of a child to the thrust and parry of sophisticated theological combat. His Marian views remain intimately bound to his Christocentric theology and to its profound consequences for both liturgy and devotional practice. Luther, even while revering Mary, grew increasingly critical of the "Papists" for obscuring the crucial distinction between noble admiration for God's grace wherever it appears in a human vessel and the rendering of religious service—properly due to God alone—to a mere creature. He judged the Roman Catholic custom of observing saints' days and directing intercessory petitions to Mary and other departed saints as nothing less than idolatry. His final reflections on Marian devotion survive in a sermon delivered at Wittenberg merely one month before death claimed him.

A digital signature constitutes a mathematical scheme through which one may verify the authenticity of messages or documents transmitted in digital form. When a valid digital signature exists—its prerequisites duly satisfied—the recipient gains very high confidence that the message originated with a known sender (authenticity), and that during its passage the message remained unaltered (integrity).

Among cryptographic protocol suites, digital signatures figure as standard elements; they find common application in software distribution, in financial transactions, in contract management software, and wherever else the detection of forgery or tampering becomes important.

Digital signatures frequently serve to implement electronic signatures—a category encompassing any electronic data that carries the intent of a signature—though not all electronic signatures employ digital signatures. In certain countries, electronic signatures possess legal significance: Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, Uruguay, Switzerland, Chile, and the nations comprising the European Union all recognize them.

The foundation of digital signatures rests upon asymmetric cryptography. In many instances, they furnish a layer of validation and security to messages dispatched through channels otherwise lacking security: properly implemented, a digital signature offers the receiver reason to believe that the claimed sender indeed transmitted the message. Digital signatures prove equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures in numerous respects, yet when properly implemented they resist forgery more effectively than their handwritten counterparts. The schemes for digital signatures, in the sense here employed, derive from cryptographic principles and demand proper implementation to achieve effectiveness. They can also provide non-repudiation, meaning the signer cannot successfully maintain they did not sign a message while simultaneously claiming their private key remains secret. Further, certain non-repudiation schemes attach a timestamp to the digital signature, ensuring that even should the private key suffer exposure, the signature retains validity. Messages bearing digital signatures may be anything representable as a bitstring: among the examples one finds electronic mail, contracts, and messages sent via other cryptographic protocols.

Control theory stands as a branch of mathematics devoted to governing the behavior of dynamical systems within the engineered processes and machines that constitute our technological world. Its central objective—to develop models or algorithms that govern how system inputs are applied—seeks to drive any given system toward a desired state while minimizing delay, overshoot, and steady-state error, ensuring meanwhile a stable level of control; frequently, the ultimate aim remains the achievement of some degree of optimality.

To accomplish this demanding task, one requires a controller equipped with the requisite corrective behavior. Such a controller monitors what is called the controlled process variable, designated PV, and compares this measured quantity against the reference value, or set point, known as SP. The difference between the actual and desired values of the process variable—this discrepancy called the error signal, or SP-PV error—is then applied as feedback, generating thereby a control action designed to bring the controlled process variable into alignment with the set point, closing the gap between intention and reality. Among other aspects subjected to rigorous study are controllability and observability, twin concepts fundamental to the discipline. Control theory finds its application in control system engineering, where it serves to design the automation systems that have revolutionized manufacturing, transformed aircraft and communications industries, and opened entirely new fields of endeavor, robotics foremost among them.

Practitioners of this discipline make extensive use of a diagrammatic convention known as the block diagram. Within such diagrams, the transfer function—also termed the system function or network function—provides a mathematical model expressing the relation between input and output, a model grounded in the differential equations that describe the system's fundamental behavior.

The lineage of control theory reaches back to the nineteenth century, when James Clerk Maxwell first articulated the theoretical basis for the operation of governors, those mechanical regulators of steam engines. Edward Routh advanced the theory further in 1874, joined by Charles Sturm and, in 1895, by Adolf Hurwitz, all contributing to the establishment of stability criteria; from 1922 onward, Nicolas Minorsky developed the foundations of PID control theory.

Though mathematical control theory finds major application in control systems engineering, its utility extends far beyond industrial process control. As the general theory of feedback systems, it proves valuable wherever feedback occurs—in the life sciences, in computer engineering, in sociology, in operations research, wherever systems require regulation and response.

Speech recognition—that interdisciplinary domain where computer science converges with computational linguistics—develops the methodologies and technologies through which machines apprehend spoken language and render it as searchable text. Known variously as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition, or speech to text (STT), this field draws upon knowledge from computer science, linguistics, and computer engineering alike, weaving these strands into a single investigative tapestry. Its mirror image, the reverse transformation, is speech synthesis: text becoming voice.

Certain systems demand what practitioners call "training" or "enrollment," a process whereby an individual speaker reads prepared text or isolated vocabulary aloud, allowing the system to analyze that particular voice's distinctive qualities and thereby refine its recognition algorithms. The result: heightened accuracy for that specific speaker. Systems dispensing with such preparation earn the designation "speaker-independent"; those requiring it are termed "speaker dependent."

The applications proliferate with remarkable variety. Voice user interfaces include voice dialing—"call home"—and call routing, as when a caller announces, "I would like to make a collect call." Domotic appliance control, keyword searches through podcasts for particular spoken words, simple data entry such as credit card numbers, preparation of structured documents like radiology reports, analysis of speaker characteristics, speech-to-text processing for word processors and emails, and aircraft systems (usually called direct voice input) all rely upon this technology.

One must distinguish voice recognition—or speaker identification—from speech recognition proper. The former identifies who speaks rather than what is spoken. Recognizing the speaker serves dual purposes: it simplifies translation in systems trained on a specific person's voice, and it authenticates or verifies a speaker's identity as part of security protocols.

From the technological vantage point, speech recognition possesses a long history punctuated by successive waves of innovation. Most recently, advances in deep learning and big data have transformed the field profoundly. Evidence of this transformation appears not merely in the proliferating academic papers flooding journals, but more significantly in the worldwide industrial adoption of diverse deep learning methodologies for designing and deploying recognition systems. The technology has arrived, and its applications continue expanding across domains previously unimaginable.

Drug design—often termed rational drug design, or simply rational design—constitutes the inventive enterprise of discovering new medications grounded in knowledge of a biological target. The drug itself most commonly takes the form of an organic small molecule, one that either activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein, thereby conferring a therapeutic benefit upon the patient. In its most fundamental sense, drug design involves fashioning molecules complementary in both shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact, ensuring that they will bind to it with specificity. Drug design frequently, though not invariably, relies upon computer modeling techniques—a practice sometimes designated as computer-aided drug design. When drug design draws upon knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target, it is known as structure-based drug design. Beyond small molecules, biopharmaceuticals—including peptides and, especially, therapeutic antibodies—represent an increasingly vital class of drugs, and computational methods for enhancing the affinity, selectivity, and stability of these protein-based therapeutics have likewise been developed and refined.

The phrase "drug design" proves, to some extent, a misnomer. A more precise term would be ligand design: the design, that is, of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target. Although design techniques for predicting binding affinity have achieved reasonable success, many other properties—bioavailability, metabolic half-life, side effects, and the like—must first be optimized before a ligand can evolve into a safe and efficacious drug. These additional characteristics often prove difficult to predict using rational design techniques alone. Nevertheless, given the high attrition rates that plague drug development, especially during its clinical phases, increasing attention is now being directed early in the drug design process toward selecting candidate drugs whose physicochemical properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development, and which are therefore more likely to culminate in an approved, marketed drug. Furthermore, in vitro experiments, when complemented by computational methods, are being employed with growing frequency in early drug discovery to identify and select compounds possessing more favorable ADME profiles—that is, absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion characteristics—as well as superior toxicological profiles.

Data dredging—known also as data snooping, or in the vernacular of contemporary research misconduct, p-hacking—constitutes a grave misuse of statistical analysis whereby investigators mine datasets for patterns that may be paraded as statistically significant, thereby inflating exponentially, while simultaneously obscuring, the true risk of false positives. The technique proceeds through a methodical exploitation: researchers perform numerous statistical tests upon their data, then selectively report only those yielding ostensibly significant results, suppressing all others.

The practice itself unfolds through systematic hypothesis testing, wherein a single dataset undergoes exhaustive interrogation. Investigators search relentlessly—now for combinations of variables that might reveal correlations, now for subgroups of cases or observations exhibiting differences in their means or in their distribution across alternative categorical breakdowns. The landscape of possible tests stretches toward infinity.

Conventional statistical significance testing rests upon a foundation of probability: it calculates the likelihood that any particular result would emerge through chance alone, and necessarily embraces some measured risk of erroneous conclusions of a specific character—namely, mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis. This accepted level of risk bears the name "significance." When researchers conduct vast numbers of tests, however, some inevitably generate false results of precisely this type. Thus five percent of randomly selected hypotheses might be erroneously proclaimed statistically significant at the five-percent significance level; one percent might be erroneously proclaimed significant at the one-percent level, and so forth—all through chance alone. When sufficient hypotheses undergo testing, it becomes virtually certain that some will appear statistically significant, though this appearance misleads, since nearly every dataset possessing any degree of randomness contains spurious correlations lurking within its structure. Researchers employing data mining techniques, if they lack caution, find themselves easily deceived by such illusory findings.

Data dredging exemplifies the broader problem of multiple comparisons disregarded. One common manifestation occurs when investigators compare subgroups without disclosing to readers the total number of subgroup comparisons they examined during their investigation.

In Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, stands Carnegie Mellon University, a private research institution whose lineage traces back to 1900, when Andrew Carnegie founded the Carnegie Technical Schools. By 1912, this enterprise had evolved into the Carnegie Institute of Technology, assuming both a new name and the authority to confer four-year degrees. The transformation that yielded the university's present identity came in 1967, when the Carnegie Institute merged with the Mellon Institute of Industrial Research—itself established in 1913 through the patronage of Andrew Mellon and Richard B. Mellon, and previously affiliated with the University of Pittsburgh. Since that union, Carnegie Mellon has functioned as one coherent academic entity.

Seven distinct colleges and schools now compose the university's structure: the College of Engineering, the College of Fine Arts, the Dietrich College of Humanities and Social Sciences, the Mellon College of Science, the Tepper School of Business, the Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy, and the School of Computer Science. Five miles from Downtown Pittsburgh lies the main campus, yet the university's reach extends far beyond western Pennsylvania. More than a dozen degree-granting locations span six continents, including substantial campuses in Qatar, Silicon Valley, and Kigali, Rwanda—the latter known as Carnegie Mellon University Africa—alongside collaborative partnerships with institutions throughout the United States and in the United Kingdom, Portugal, Japan, China, Mexico, and Italy.

Carnegie Mellon has distinguished itself through pioneering scholarship and the cultivation of emerging disciplines. The university claims particular renown in computer science, having established the first departments devoted to that field, to machine learning, and to robotics. It advanced the discipline of management science and inaugurated the first drama program in the United States. Classified among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very High Research Activity," the institution reported research and development expenditures of $386 million in 2020 alone. Among its faculty and alumni—past and present—number twenty Nobel Prize laureates, thirteen Turing Award recipients, twenty-six members of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, thirty-nine fellows of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, ninety-one members of the National Academies, one hundred forty-two Emmy Award winners, fifty-two Tony Award laureates, and twelve Academy Award winners. The university enrolls 15,818 students from 117 countries across its global campuses, employs more than 1,400 faculty members, and maintains an alumni community exceeding 112,000.

You long, perhaps, for a mother who might prove sweet and gentle, understanding in her gestures, kind in her approach to the world. But whatever your disappointments, however justified your grievances, guard against disrespect; above all, do not give voice to these feelings in her presence. Such confessions will only deepen your predicament. There exists a considerable likelihood that your mother knows full well the limits of her intelligence, and this painful self-knowledge drives her toward cruelty. To remind her of these deficiencies, to hold them up like accusations, will purchase you nothing but greater suffering.

After you have granted yourself permission to weep, to shout, to release whatever storm builds inside you, withdraw from the immediate grip of emotion. Among the more constructive approaches to managing your relationship with your mother stands emotional detachment—a studied distance from which you can operate. No anger, no whining, no crying or begging or yelling or belittlement: only facts, delivered plainly. When she acts with deliberate intent to wound you or provoke your rage, your most effective defense becomes a refusal to feel wounded or enraged at all.

Insofar as circumstances allow, complete what she desires before she articulates the demand. This strategy removes one potential source of her meanness while granting you leverage when the moment arrives to request something for yourself.

Observe with care the perspectives offered by your friends' mothers, those women who demonstrate greater gentleness, consistency, responsibility. Seek information beyond your household walls. Much of what you absorb daily works to sabotage your understanding and may prove fundamentally mistaken. Rather than merely nursing anger at her misguidance, pursue better sources of wisdom and commit their lessons to memory. Question everything she asserts about your character or about existence itself; measure her pronouncements against what ministers say, what therapists suggest, what teachers explain, what healthier adults model. Examine the full architecture of your life, for these patterns do not erupt from nowhere. They travel through generations like heirlooms, and you need not continue passing them forward.

Family dynamics can be studied—there exist books devoted to the subject—and such study helps you comprehend the system while choosing your own direction. Your mother may grow angrier still when you cease responding to familiar manipulations in the expected manner, but building this interior resistance remains essential to protecting both mind and soul.

Do not register surprise when she accuses you of transgressions you would never contemplate. If such behaviors belong to her repertoire, she assumes they belong to yours, regardless of truth. Cruel mothers rarely maintain firm purchase on reality; they cannot distinguish your good conduct from misbehavior. The wisest course remains behaving well regardless, while cultivating relationships with others who can witness the situation directly.

The grizzly and the black bear demand divergent strategies of defense. Vigilance serves as your first protection; never position yourself between a sow and her offspring.

The black bear presents itself in deceptive variety—its coat may appear black as char, russet brown, or the warm tone of ground cinnamon. Typically more compact in frame, it possesses sharply tapered ears and lacks the characteristic shoulder mass that distinguishes its larger cousin.

The grizzly, by contrast, wears fur ranging from deep brown through honey blonde to an almost silvered cast. A pronounced muscular hump rises between its shoulders; its face forms a concave profile, bowl-like in curvature, and its ears describe rounded shapes against the skull. At maturity, the grizzly surpasses the black bear considerably in size.

Both species possess olfactory powers of extraordinary refinement, their sensitive nostrils constantly sampling the wind. Through summer's abundance and autumn's urgent preparation, they forage without cease, driven by the imperative of accumulating reserves.

Bear spray—a specialized deterrent—projects a cone of aerosolized capsaicin extending thirty feet from the canister. Deploy this tool only when a charging bear thunders toward you, only when you must alter the animal's trajectory at the critical moment.

Position your bear spray where your hand can seize it instantly. Familiarize yourself with the trigger mechanism before need transforms practice into necessity.

Discharge the spray when the approaching bear closes to within forty feet of your position.

Never employ bear spray as prophylactic measure. Its formulation achieves such potency that applying it to gear or clothing invites disaster rather than prevents it.

Human voices, sustained and unmistakable, repel both grizzlies and black bears from contested ground. Bear bells tinkle with insufficient volume to achieve meaningful deterrence, but conversation between hikers accomplishes what metal chimes cannot. Solitude compounds vulnerability in bear country; if companionship proves unavailable or if you prefer silence to speech, carry a satellite radio tuned to programming featuring human dialogue. A lone figure attracts ursine attention more readily than a group moving together.

Bears achieve velocities reaching thirty-five miles per hour—speeds that render human flight absurd. They climb trees with facility and swim with power.

Proper food storage in bear-resistant, airtight containers prevents scent dispersal. Negligence here transforms your presence from neutral to attractive, summoning rather than repelling.

When encountering a bear, maintain your position while generating noise; avert your gaze to avoid challenge.

Bears occasionally rear onto hind legs for improved observation—a gesture of curiosity rather than aggression. Project confidence; hold your ground.

A small black bear's assault might permit defensive resistance.

Against a grizzly, assume the fetal position immediately, fingers interlaced behind your neck for protection. Stillness may persuade the animal of your harmlessness or apparent death, prompting withdrawal.

Bear attacks remain,

Consult your physician regarding the advisability of taking your customary morning medications on the day of the procedure. Should you live with diabetes, inquire specifically whether insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents may be administered before the examination commences. Similarly, disclose to your doctor any documented history of asthma, renal insufficiency, or disorders affecting coagulation and hemostasis. These particular conditions may necessitate special precautionary measures, modifications to standard protocols, or enhanced monitoring throughout the procedure to ensure your safety and minimize potential complications during the examination itself.

In the days preceding your scheduled angiogram, you may receive instructions to discontinue aspirin—including any pharmaceutical preparations or over-the-counter remedies containing this antiplatelet agent—as well as prescription anticoagulants and blood-thinning medications. Engage in thorough discussion with your physician to establish precisely when these medications may be safely resumed following the completion of your procedure.

Women who are pregnant require particular caution when contemplating certain medical interventions, given the imperative to avoid potential harm to the developing fetus. If you are pregnant, suspect you might be carrying a child, or have recently given birth, share these crucial details with your physician so that together you may deliberate upon and determine the most judicious course of action. It becomes extraordinarily important to disclose pregnancy status when an angiogram proves medically necessary to detect possible coronary artery obstruction or blockage. Such findings may subsequently require therapeutic intervention through reperfusion techniques and stenting procedures designed to restore adequate blood flow to cardiac tissue and preserve myocardial function.

Should you be nursing an infant, employ infant formula for one to two days following your angiogram, allowing sufficient time for the contrast dye to pass completely through your system before resuming breastfeeding.

Your physician will establish which preliminary tests and diagnostic procedures you must undergo before your angiogram can be performed. Ensure that you adhere meticulously to your doctor's directives and complete all recommended testing without delay or omission. These preparatory measures may include phlebotomy for laboratory analysis or an electrocardiogram to assess baseline cardiac electrical activity.

Iodine-based contrast dye typically serves as the imaging agent during cardiac catheterization procedures. Your physician must be informed if you possess an allergy to iodine so that alternative treatment options and contrast media may be explored and evaluated. Certain substitute dyes may provoke allergic reactions in individuals with documented shellfish sensitivities, making disclosure of such allergies equally essential.

Most angiographic procedures are scheduled during morning hours, rendering fasting requirements less burdensome an inconvenience. Nevertheless, abstaining from food and beverages constitutes an important element of proper preparation for your angiogram and must be observed conscientiously. Should your examination be scheduled for an afternoon or later time slot, refrain from consuming any food or drink for four to eight hours preceding the test.

In the hours before your procedure—most critically during the twenty-four-hour period immediately preceding it—you should scrupulously avoid both alcohol and tobacco products. These substances can impair your judgment and behavior, alter physiological parameters and test results, and precipitate various complications during the procedure itself. If sedative medications are administered during your angiogram, their effects may be dangerously intensified by any alcohol remaining in your system.

Inform your doctor comprehensively about all medications you currently take, encompassing prescription pharmaceuticals, over-the-counter preparations, herbal remedies, and nutritional supplements. Bring these medications in their original labeled containers to your consultation. This practice will aid your memory and ensure complete disclosure of your pharmaceutical regimen. Remember also to notify your physician about any medications to which you have demonstrated allergic reactions or adverse responses.

Though the angiogram represents a relatively straightforward procedure, you must arrive at the hospital prepared as though for surgery. Appropriate preparation includes observing your doctor's instructions regarding dietary intake during the twenty-four hours before your procedure—which typically means consuming nothing by mouth during the six to eight hours immediately preceding it. Remove contact lenses, eyeglasses, hair accessories, nail polish, and jewelry before the test begins; ideally, leave jewelry at home to prevent loss. Empty your bladder before the examination commences, as the procedure can require several hours to complete.

Upon arrival at the hospital, you will check in and confer with your medical team, who will explain precisely what will transpire during the procedure so you feel adequately prepared. They will apprise you of any possible complications or risks associated with the examination. Subsequently, you will be escorted to a preparation area where you can change into a hospital gown before the procedure begins.

Following most angiographic procedures, patients remain at the facility for four to six hours, during which medical staff observe you carefully to detect any postoperative complications. During this recovery interval, endeavor to relax completely. Avoid dwelling anxiously upon the results. Simply enjoy this enforced respite while physicians and nurses monitor your condition.

Sedative medications may be administered during or immediately before your angiogram. These drugs will impair your cognitive functioning and ability to operate motor vehicles safely. Arrange for a trusted companion to transport you home and assist you in settling in after your procedure. Ideally, this person should remain with you for several hours—preferably overnight—in case you require assistance. Most medical facilities maintain policies refusing to perform angiograms on patients who lack a responsible adult committed to accompanying them home afterward.

Rest constitutes one of the most effective means of facilitating bodily recovery from any medical procedure. Adequate rest promotes healing and helps prevent potential complications. Following your angiogram, you will likely experience some discomfort in the groin area where the catheter was inserted. Bed rest minimizes movement in this region, allowing proper healing. Plan to remain home for several days following the procedure to ensure adequate convalescence.

Discuss with your physician any questions or concerns regarding the procedure, your recovery, and the test results. Communicate candidly about your physical sensations and any difficulties you have encountered. Inquire about the outcome and its implications for your future health: Will additional testing be required? Does your condition necessitate surgical intervention? Should you modify aspects of your lifestyle?
